content.intro: This lesson covers rag evaluation through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Build RAG as a chain of data preparation, retrieval, context assembly, generation, source attribution, and evaluation; inspect each stage instead of treating it as a single prompt.
content.why_it_matters: Retrieval precision and recall concerns how content is represented, selected, or ranked for relevance. Keep the source text and metadata traceable, measure retrieval with labeled queries, and verify that similarity scores correspond to useful results rather than assuming nearby vectors prove factual correctness.

items.title: End-to-end evaluation
items.text: Use end-to-end evaluation to turn a vague quality claim into an observable criterion. Define a representative dataset, an expected outcome or rubric, a baseline, and the failure categories you will record; interpret aggregate scores alongside examples and affected groups.

content_blocks.code:
# Focus: RAG Evaluation
relevant = {"d1", "d2"}
retrieved = ["d2", "d3", "d1"]
precision = len(set(retrieved) & relevant) / len(retrieved)
recall = len(set(retrieved) & relevant) / len(relevant)
print({"precision": round(precision, 3), "recall": round(recall, 3)})

content.task: Practice retrieval precision and recall within rag evaluation: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
